text:
Predicates:
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
Schedule(x, y) ::: x schedules a meeting with y.
Customer(y) ::: y is a customer.
GoToCompanyBuilding(x) ::: x goes to the company building.
HasLunch(x, y) ::: x has lunch in y.
CompanyBuilding(y) ::: y is the company building.
Home(y) ::: y is home.
WorkRemotelyFromHome(x) ::: x works remotely from home.
InOtherCountries(x) ::: x is in other countries.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
AppearInCompanyToday(x) ::: x appears in the company today.

Premises:
∀x (∀y (Schedule(x, y) ∧ Customer(y)) → GoToCompanyBuilding(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will go to the company building today.
∀x (HasLunch(x, companyBuilding) → ∃y (Schedule(x, y) ∧ Customer(y))) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company building schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (HasLunch(x, companyBuilding) ⊕ HasLunch(x, home)) ::: Employees have lunch either in the company building or at home.
∀x (HasLunch(x, home) → WorkRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, they are working remotely from home.
∀x (InOtherCountries(x) → WorkRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
¬∃x (Manager(x) ∧ WorkRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
AppearInCompanyToday(james) ↔ Manager(james) ::: James will appear in the company today if and only if he is a manager.

Conclusion:
(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountries(james)) → ¬(HasLunch(james, home) ∨ WorkRemotelyFromHome(james)) ::: If James is either a manager or in other countries, then James does not either have lunch at home or work remotely from home.
(HasLunch(james, home) ∨ WorkRemotelyFromHome(james)) → ¬(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountries(james)) ::: If James either has lunch at home or works remotely from home, then he is neither a manager nor does he work in other countries.
